title: Message Passing on the Edge: Scalable Graph Learning
one_liner: Instead of updating nodes by talking to their neighbors, update edges by counting triangles they belong to, and stay fast while being smarter.
lead: Most graph neural networks talk between neighboring nodes, passing information up the connection lines. But nodes are limited: they only know about their immediate circle. This paper flips the view and puts the conversation on the edges themselves. Each edge (connection) asks: what triangles include me? By answering that question efficiently, the model can tell more graph patterns apart, without slowing down.

paras: In a real network (a social graph, a molecule, a road map), the connections between things matter more than the things themselves. A graph neural network reads a graph by placing a small number-list on each node (assigning each node a list of numbers that carries learned information), then has nodes swap information with their direct neighbors, layer by layer. Each node learns from what its neighbors know.

The trouble: a node only knows about its immediate circle. Imagine three nodes A, B, C all connected in a triangle. A node cannot tell a triangle from a star just by counting neighbors; a star has three points but is not a triangle. So these networks miss important patterns. Researchers tested this limit carefully and found a boundary called the 1WL test (a game where one player paints nodes and the other tries to tell graphs apart). Vertex-based message passing cannot see past this line, no matter how many layers you add.

callout.html: Nodes only know their neighbors, so they miss patterns that need looking at edges and triangles.

panels.title: 5. Edges become smarter
panels.caption: Edges in triangles stay active; fresh edges also matter. Model sees more patterns.

steps.text: Run a fast scan to mark which edges sit inside triangles (a connection with both endpoints sharing a common neighbor).

steps.b: Place features on edges, not nodes
steps.text: Give each ordered edge a number-list, tracking what the edge represents.

steps.b: Color edges by their triangle role
steps.text: Each edge learns the multiset of how many triangles it touches and what colors those triangles have from the last layer.
Each edge gathers info from edges that share an endpoint or sit in the same triangle, computing their intersection pattern.
Feed the aggregated triangle info through a small neural net to get the new edge number-list, ready for the next layer.

paras: The paper shifts the core building block from nodes to edges. A node's number-list was a fixed snapshot at each vertex. An edge's number-list is assigned to each connection, and it rides the message-passing updates layer by layer. Instead of nodes talking, edges talk.
object.object: the message carrier (from nodes to edges)

hidden.name: Triangle membership color count
paras: The hidden quantity is the fingerprint of which and how many triangles each edge belongs to. It is not a single number but a multiset: the collection of colors (states) that the triangles containing this edge held at the previous layer. Two edges in structurally similar positions (both in two triangles of the same color) will have the same fingerprint.

The paper estimates this by running the Chiba-Nishizeki algorithm once at the start (a fast scan that lists all triangles in near-linear time), then during message passing, each edge explicitly counts the colors of its neighboring edges and triangle structures. This fingerprint lets the model tell apart graphs that vertex-based methods cannot, because two edges in structurally identical local neighborhoods (same triangle counts, same surrounding colors) will compute identical updates, but a vertex-based model might miss this since a node only sees its neighbors, not the triangles within them.

heat.caption: Edges in many triangles (e1, e2, e4, e8, e11) stay hot; fresh or lonely edges stay cool. The heat is the triangle count from the edge's neighborhood.

reads.html: An edge remembers how many triangles surround it and what those triangles looked like in the previous round. Two edges with the same triangle memory look identical to the model.

The multiset C_τ of colors computed by EB-1WL after t steps belonging to each triangle τ in Γ(G). The new color of edge {u, v} is completely determined by the triangle membership and the colors it observes.

mechanism.h2: Why triangles make the model smarter
paras: The root idea: a node only sees its neighbors, but an edge sees more. An edge between nodes u and v has two endpoints, and if they share a common neighbor w, then u, v, w form a triangle. That triangle is local to the edge but invisible to the node. By writing the message-passing rules on edges instead of nodes, the model can directly measure and react to triangles.

Here is the causal chain. First, the model needs to distinguish graphs that differ in their triangle structure. Vertex-based methods cannot do this because they update nodes in isolation. Second, edges are located exactly at the junctions where triangles form (the intersection of two node neighborhoods). Third, by having each edge track the colors of its triangles, the model sees the precise local structure. Fourth, when two edges sit in structurally equivalent positions (same number of triangles, same colors), they get the same update, so the model can group them correctly. This grouping is exactly what the 1WL test measures, and triangle-aware edge grouping can distinguish more graph pairs than 1WL can, because the test now runs on edges that see triangles rather than nodes that see only neighbors.

Computationally, the Chiba-Nishizeki algorithm runs once as a preprocessing step in near-linear time, so the triangles do not have to be rediscovered every layer. The message passing itself is also near-linear per edge (each edge talks to its neighbors and triangles), so the wall-clock time stays reasonable even on large sparse graphs. The reason this is faster: instead of each node gathering info from all its neighbors (which could be many), each edge gathers info from only the triangles it belongs to, which is typically far fewer.

stages.s: Raw graph with edges marked as triangle or not
Each edge gathers colors from its triangles
Compute multiset of triangle colors (the fingerprint)
Update edge number-list via neural network
New edge number-lists ready for next layer

math.words: The new color of an edge depends on its old color and the multiset of colors of all triangles it belongs to. Formally: the new color f at layer i+1 of edge (u,v) is computed by hashing together the old color of (u,v) and the sorted list of colors of each triangle τ that contains (u,v) at layer i.
math.equation: f^(i+1)(u,v) = HASH( f^(i)(u,v), SORT( { color^(i)(τ) : (u,v) ∈ τ } ) )
symbols: the embedding (feature vector) of edge (u,v) at layer i
the color (state) assigned to triangle τ at layer i
the set of triangles that contain the edge (u,v)
sort the multiset to make it order-independent
a deterministic function that maps the combined input to the new embedding

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose edge (A,B) is in two triangles (A,B,C) and (A,B,D).
At layer 0: f^0(A,B) = [0.5, 0.3], color^0(A,B,C) = red, color^0(A,B,D) = red.
Multiset of triangle colors: {red, red}. After SORT: [red, red].
Edge (A,B) now has number-list [0.7, 0.2] at layer 1, learned from its two red triangles.

math.note: The multiset of triangle colors is the triangle fingerprint; the HASH function (usually an injective neural network) ensures edges in the same local roles get similar number-lists.

charts.title: Vertex-based message passing (standard MPNN)
charts.note: Can only reach 1WL expressivity limit; struggles on large graphs.

charts.title: Edge-based message passing (EB-GNN)
charts.note: Reaches higher expressivity via triangle awareness; fast due to near-linear scaling.

items.b: Triangle enumeration cost on dense graphs.
items.html: The Chiba-Nishizeki algorithm is near-linear in the number of edges, but on dense graphs (many triangles per edge), the preprocessing can still be slow. The paper is optimized for sparse, real-world graphs.
If the task only requires learning node properties (like simple node classification), the extra triangle awareness adds cost without benefit. Edge message-passing is not a universal speedup.

items.b: Ordered edges mean more values to store.
items.html: The model has a number-list for each directed edge: one for u to v and another for v to u separately. In undirected graphs this can double the feature count and memory. The paper handles this via weight-sharing, but the overhead is real.

On sparse graphs where triangle structure matters (molecular graphs, social networks, knowledge graphs), the method is both faster and more accurate than standard message-passing networks, because sparse graphs have few triangles per edge (the triangle count stays manageable even though the graph is large), and triangles encode the essential local structure that the task cares about.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a graph comparison task: create two small graphs that are provably different in their triangle structure (for example, a star graph and a triangle graph, both with 4 nodes). Train a standard vertex-based GNN and an edge-based EB-GNN side-by-side to classify which is which. The demo should show that the edge model learns to separate them in fewer layers, while the vertex model plateaus at random guessing (50% accuracy), because the edge model sees the triangle directly while the node model only counts neighbors. Then measure wall-clock time and peak memory on a real 10K-node graph and confirm EB-GNN is faster, because the triangle enumeration is done once and each edge gathers from only its triangles (a smaller set than all neighbors).
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss: edges know about triangles, and that knowledge is both more accurate (because triangles encode local structure vertex-based methods cannot access) and faster to compute on real graphs (because triangles are counted once, then reused, while nodes must repeatedly query all neighbors).
